subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
In my opinion the chairman and the committee which brought in this report are to be congratulated upon the fine piece of work they have done. They have completed a thorough job and brought in a unanimous report embodying thirty-six conclusions and recommendations which the house should speedily pass for governmental action. The committee was composed of members of every group in the house, and the report was unanimous; why then should there be any delay in implementing the recommendations? The House of Commons appointed this select special committee on February 1, 1937, to continue and complete the inquiry begun the year before by the standing committee on agriculture. The report was presented to parliament on April 7, 1937, and the understanding then was that the house would be asked to express an opinion at the present session.
While the inquiry was national in scope, the problem is peculiarly acute in western Canada, and the position of western agriculture is emphasized in the report, although full consideration was given to the whole country.
Some trouble apparently arises from the fact that nearly all the Canadian companies manufacturing farm implements are located in the province of Ontario, so to the other difficulties under which western Canadian and maritime farmers suffer is added the cost of freight, and there have been indeed many other difficulties to which it can be added.
As regards the condition of agriculture in the last decade, let me quote from page 1217 of the report:
It needs little argument to support the general statement that the economic condition of agriculture since 1929 has been extremely bad. Almost every factor that could possibly affect the position of the farmer has operated to his disadvantage during that period. In western Canada the coincidence of poor crops over a long period and of abnormally low prices for farm products, combined with unfavourable world and local conditions, made the farmers position a particularly unfavourable one. While industry attempted to restrict its losses by decreased production, entailing the laying on of employees, the reduction of expenses, and by the maintenance of prices for its product, the farmer, by virtue of being forced to market his products at prices largely determined by agencies other than himself, has had very little control of the financial results of his industry.
Note these phrases: "Coincidence of poor crops over a long period and of abnormally low prices for farm products. This combination of factors would be disastrous enough alone, but note what accompanied them. 
Those factors, "combined with unfavourable world and local conditions," as we are told, could not fail to make "the farmer's position a particularly unfavourable one."
We know that both dominion and provincial governments stepped in and spent large sums of money by way of relief to keep the farmer in business, and large sums to stabilize agricultural conditions in parts of Canada. And, to quote again, the committee felt, or hoped:
.	.	. that it is quite fair and proper topoint out to the farm implement manufacturers that these governments are spending such sums in order to keep the farmers, who constitute the customers of the farm implement industry, on their farms, and to stabilize and improve their condition. It is therefore not too much to expect the farm implement companies, who will indirectly benefit thereby, to make a substantial contribution toward the same end, and that this contribution should consist of supplying the farmers of Canada with the implements of production at the lowest possible price .	.	.
That was indeed a pious hope of the committee, but apparently one of those hopes deferred that make the heart sick. Was that expressed hope of the committee well founded? Did the wish fall on receptive ears? Was the hope fulfilled by the future actions of the farm implement manufacturers? Let events occurring since that time be the answer. This report was brought to the house on April 7, 1937, and before that summer was over the farm implement manufacturers further advanced their prices by 7-8 per cent. That is how they answered the hope of the committee.
The committee also studied the financial structure and results of the principal implement companies from 1926 to 1935. They delved exhaustively into costs, prices and distribution of implements and repairs and parts over a large range. These matters are all set out and analyzed in many instructive charts, which well repay study. On the matter of repairs the finding is significant and well worth quoting. It is found on page 1275:
It should be kept in mind that the use of "repairs" is the "poor man's" method of keeping his implements in good condition when his financial position will not permit him to purchase a new machine, and that every effort should be made by the companies to keep the price of these repair parts as low as possible. This, in the opinion of the committee, the companies have signally failed to do.
Surely no comment is needed on that.

Farm Implements Committee Report
The committee also looked into the matter of tariffs, and made some pertinent statements on this subject. Here is one on page 1288:
The committee is of the opinion after considering all of the evidence submitted that a reduction in tariff undoubtedly should, and actually does, in the long run, operate to reduce to the lowest competitive figure the ultimate price to the consumer.
Again at page 1291 we find this summing up of the portion of the report dealing with the effects of tariffs and trade barriers:
To sum up, therefore, the committee is of the opinion that the reduction on tariffs should find its full effect in a comparative reduction in price levels unless the element of true competition is lacking. If this element is lacking it nullifies to some extent the natural effect of such reduction.
They go much further than that in the case of one implement, the cream separator. They recommend without reservation, in paragraph 16 appearing on page 1295, that cream separators be placed on the free list. On Tuesday, March 15, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) dealt exhaustively and exclusively with the question of cream separators and made out what I considered, and other hon. members agreed, was an unanswerable case for cream separators being placed on the free list. The complete case for making cream separators duty free is embodied, I submit, in that speech.
Then in paragraph 17 we find this:
That reduction in the tariff should and does, in the long run, tend to lower the price level to the farmer, depending on the extent of free price competition in the industry.
In view of the findings of the committee; in view of all the information upon which those findings were based, and above all in view of the action of the implement manufacturers in impudently flouting the government and the committee by increasing prices in 1936, with a further increase of 7-8 per cent last summer, after this report was presented to parliament, which increase means a new and unjustifiable levy of around $4,000,000 on the farmers of the prairies alone for the benefit of the makers of the tools they use, I cannot see why these implements should not be placed on the free list, and why resolution No. 17 should not read in that way.
In closing, may I quote short extracts from two letters received within the last few days, which set forth the considered opinion of the thinking farmers in this country:
The report of the special committee of last year, they feel, is a call to action which ought not to be ignored, and there seems to be no action in sight just now. They view this with
extreme disappointment. That a widespread injustice should not only he permitted to continue but actually be allowed to increase creates a very grave situation.
Then, from the other letter:
We are very much concerned about this situation. The implement people appear determined to over-ride the conclusions and recommendations of last year's committee and to press still more extortionate prices in 1938. We think this is a challenge to Canadian democracy and we are looking for unified action on the part of the representatives of rural Canada.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, that is the situation. Action is called for here, definite, effective and undelayed. That action should be, on the part of the government, to wipe out all duties on all farm implements.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the discussion of the report of the special committee appointed to investigate prices of farm implements, my first thought is to avail myself of this opportunity to extend my congratulations to Mr. Graham, the solicitor, and Mr. Macdonald, the chartered accountant, upon their untiring efforts and effective work, which greatly facilitated the investigation.
The point that interests me most in respect to this matter is the present extremely high price of farm implements, especially when compared with the past and prevailing prices of the products which the farmer must sell in order to pay for the implements required to operate his farm. The object of this investigation was not to set the farmer against the implement manufacturer or vice versa, but, through a complete survey of the entire question relative to the manufacture, transportation and distribution of farm implements, to ascertain whether or not the increase made early in 1936 in the prices of this type of farm equipment was justified, and, if not. what action within the scope of governmental jurisdiction might be undertaken to assist in reducing the cost of these implements. I am aware that power is not vested in governments to state at what prices produce or equipment or goods must be sold within or without the boundaries of our country. In fact, I am not one of those who believes in regimentation or government control of agriculture, industry or business. Yet governments have control of fiscal policy, which is an instrument that may be used to promote the best interests of the greatest number of people.
I now come to a point which must not be forgotten. I refer to the necessity of maintaining the lowest possible price for all implements used in the production of natural
2590	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
wealth by means of agriculture, mining and forestry. The prosperity of this dominion depends to a large extent upon the development of our natural resources. Huge quantities of implements and machinery are required for this purpose, and in my opinion it is the duty of the government to see that everything possible is done to prevent exploitation of the producers of natural wealth through extremely high implement and machine prices.
The argument has been heard in recent debates on this question that the cost of farm implements represents a very minor expense to the farmer. I take strong exception to this assumption. The cost of the ordinary group of farm implements to be found on the average Ontario farm-and in this connection I am referring to the horse-drawn type of implement, thereby eliminating tractor or power machines-would amount to approximately SI,800. During his lifetime the average farmer will wear out two outfits. Add to this the high cost of repairs, and I am confident hon. members will agree with me that this represents a major item of expense to the farmer. In support of that contention I might say that on my farm I am using my third plough, my second binder and my second mower, so I feel that this statement is quite within the bounds of reason and truth. If we take the net income of the average farmer in the province of Ontario as given to this house by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), amounting to S365 a year, if my memory serves me correctly, it is not hard to figure out how long a farmer spends during his lifetime working to pay for these implements.
I come to another point which I desire to bring to the attention of the house. If during the period when the sale of implements almost reached the vanishing point, due to the greatly diminished purchasing power of the farmer, the implement companies had substantially reduced the prices of farm implements, this would have stimulated the purchase of these implements, which would have resulted in greater profits for the implement manufacturers and increased employment for those engaged in the implement industry.
In connection with credit or time sales there seemed to be ample justification for the implement companies to provide for an increase in the percentage of the cash or down payment, as it is commonly called; yet, in my opinion an exorbitant rate of interest is charged the farmers for the balance of the time payments. Furthermore, in recent years this cost has been materially increased. Let

us take what might be described as staple implements on an Ontario farm, namely a binder, a disc drill, a mower, a ten foot rake and a four section harrow. The per annum rate oif interest prevailing in connection with time payments on these machines for 140 to 180 days will amount to at least 16 per cent, a rate of interest which, I am sure the house will agree, is much too high.
In order to determine the true position of the farmer with respect to an exchange of the product of his labour for the implements required to operate his farm, I shall place on record approximate figures covering this point for the years 1913, 1926 and 1936. For this purpose I am using two typical implements used on an Ontario farm.

speechtext:
Yes; they are a six foot mower and a 13-run single disc drill. As regards farm produce, for the purpose suggested I am using two items produced extensively in Ontario, namely butcher cattle and butter fat, based on the market price at Toronto.
In 1913, 1,008 pounds of butcher cattle were required to purchase a six foot mower, while in 1926 1,600 pounds were required, and in 1936, 2,373 pounds. In connection with the disc drill we find that in 1913, 1,391 pounds of butcher cattle were required to purchase the drill, while in 1926, 2,464 pounds were required, and in 1936, 3,407 pounds.
Then, covering the same point, and using butter for the purchase of these two machines, we find that in 1913, 205 pounds of butter fat were required to purchase a six foot mower, while in 1926, 244 pounds were required, and in 1936, 423 pounds. In connection with the drill we find that in 1913, 267 pounds of butter fat were required to make the purchase, while in 1926, 376 pounds were required, and in 1936, 608 pounds.
I come now to the recommendations of the committee with respect to placing cream separators on the free list. In this connection may I say that during the debate some objections have been made with respect to the amount of time given by the committee to representatives of companies manufacturing cream separators to present their views. I am of opinion that sufficient time was allowed to cover the important points, in addition to'the information secured by correspondence with the interested companies.
I shall now proceed to give comparative figures in connection with cream separators, on approximately the same basis as that used a few minutes ago with respect to typical

Farm Implements Committee Report
farm implements. We find that in 1913, the proceeds from the sale of 320 pounds of butter fat were required to purchase a No. 16 De Laval cream separator, while in 1926, 250 pounds were required and in 1936, 430 pounds.
In connection with costs in the production of cream separators I understand the costs of the De Laval Company consist largely of materials purchased from the parent company in the United States or Sweden. According to information filed with the committee this item amounted to $50 for the No. 16 separator. The labour cost on each separator in the Canadian plant amounts to only $1.64. Therefore this company cannot do a very great deal of manufacturing in Canada in connection with the production of cream separators. The Canadian plant is in reality only an assembly plant. I would not be surprised to find that as a result of this situation substantial profits are retained by the parent company in either or both of the countries referred to, thus affecting the profit of the local company.
In view of these circumstances there seems to be ample justification for the attitude taken by the committee in recommending that cream separators be placed upon the free list. During the afternoon and formerly in this debate much has been said with respect to cooperation and unity in Canada. No one is more anxious than I am to promote sentiment of that kind. But let us consider what the farmer, the farmer's wife, son or daughter who turned a cream separator from 1931 until the first of this year received by way of an hourly wage. What did they receive for the labour expended in that operation? The answer is, far below a living wage. I am free to admit that in the months of January, February and March of 1938 butter fat did reach a substantial and profitable price. In my remarks I do not desire in any way to speak disparagingly of any citizens of the dominion or with respect, particularly, to those of the city of Toronto. But what did we find? We found that when butter reached thirty-eight or forty cents a pound, the women of that city banded themselves together to force down the price. I maintain that if we are going to develop unity in Canada, we are fully justified under such circumstances in rising in our places in the house and defending the rights and needs of those engaged in butter fat production in this province of Ontario.
In view of the foregoing facts it is not surprising that agriculture enjoyed prosperous times in 1926, because there existed
at that time a reasonable balance of value between the farmers' sales of produce and their purchases of machinery and other commodities, I am sure the house will agree that the prosperity in the period referred to was not confined to the agricultural population, but was enjoyed to the same extent by all citizens of the dominion.
In order to determine whether the suggested increase in price early in 1936 was justified, or not, I shall make an analysis of the total costs in manufacturing implements in Canada in the years 1934 and 1935. We shall divide the costs into three classifications, namely, material, labour, and burden, based on 100 per cent of the net sales realization. In 1934, the cost of material amounted to 40-22 per cent, the cost of labour, 11-1 per cent, and the cost of burden-which means all other items entering into the cost of the implement-to 35-82 per cent making a total for that year of 87-05 per cent of the net sales realization.
In 1935 the cost of material amounted to 37-08 per cent; the cost of labour, 9-92 per cent, and the cost of burden, 19-75 per cent, or a total of 66-75 per cent of the net sales realization. A comparison of the costs for the above-mentioned periods fully demonstrates that the suggestion of the implement companies to increase prices may be described as absolutely unwarranted.
Mr. Speaker, a discussion of this question would not be complete without reference to the budget of 1936 when the duty on farm implements was reduced to its present level of approximately 7i per cent. One cannot recall the discussion which took place in the house at that time without remembering the fear and apprehension which prevailed in the minds of some of the ihon, members to my immediate left. May I direct attention to some of the remarks made at that time by the hon. member for Greenwood, whose family has had a long and distinguished connection with the agricultural implement industry in several important countries throught the world. The hon. member is reported at page 2539 of Hansard of 1936 as follows:
The reduction of the duty on farm implements to 7J per cent does one thing and one thing only; it spells disaster to the implement industry of Canada. This means that the jobs of 18,000 men are threatened by the introduction of this tariff.
The hon. member is also reported on the same page as having stated that his chief interest was not in the implement industry, but in the men employed in that industry and their jobs.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to make a speech, but I am going to state a few facts and draw my own conclusions.
I visited a farm twenty-two miles west of Fort William, and I saw a separator which had done its work and was being cleaned up for duty again. I saw five gallons of cream in a can, and I asked1 the farmer how much he would get for it. He said, "Eighty cents." I was appalled. Five gallons of cream for eighty cents 1 And as I sit in this house and listen to the minister trying to induce the youth of Canada to take up farm life, I wish he would take a peek into that can of cream -five gallons for eighty cents. Those who have been brought up on a farm know what work that means. It meant many a tired hand. It meant getting up early in the morning; it meant the care of cattle, long hours of work. I do not say that is an argument against the price of separators, but I do say it is an inducement to protect not the seller of the separator but rather the man who buys it. I know something of organized labour, and I know it is pretty well able to take care of itself, but those who work on the farm have not been able to take care of themselves. The man in the factory works eight hours a day and gets at least forty cents an hour, but the young man on the farm could hardly make a living if he worked only eight hours a day. He works more like ten or twelve hours a day and more, and he does not get forty cents an hour. It would take many a can of milk to show enough profit to buy a pair of overalls for the farmer or a new hat for his wife.
We are told that the farmers in the west, as I view them in southern Saskatchewan, should be induced to go into mixed farming, but I would ask those who urge the farmers to do that to take a peek at that five gallons of cream for eighty cents.

speechtext: Eighty cents a gallon?

speechtext: No. Who should be protected-the manufacturer who makes the machine or the man who uses it? I congratulate the committee most earnestly upon the encouragement it gives to our farmers in recommending that cream separators and other implements be put on the free list.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on this motion for concurrence in the report of the special committee that has been considering the high price of farm implements. So many have spoken already in this debate that it is difficult to avoid touching on some things which have already been discussed, but I noticed this afternoon that the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) stated that during the period from 1890 to 1935 the implement manufacturers in Canada had merely made a profit of 3J per cent on the stock issued by these companies during that period.
To put before the house what the position of the implement manufacturer is, may I be permitted to state that one company merged with other manufacturers in 1891 with a capital of approximately 83,500,000, plus $1,000,000 added later, about 1911, and what has been the result for this company? In the period from 1891 to 1912 the following profits were made, and I am giving these figures because I want to show, in answer to what was put on the record by the hon. member for Haldimand, that in some periods the farm implement manufacturers have been fortunate enough to make large profits. The company in question paid cash dividends to the amount of SI 1.212,349; stock dividends to the amount of $8,500,000; a rest account was created of $6,500,000, and a special contingency account set up of $1,680,000. In addition, there were unallocated profits of $1,062,000, or a total of $28,959,349 on an investment of $3,500,000, plus $1,000,000 invested later. All that was made in a period of about twenty-one years, and when we are considering the whole situation in regard to the high prices of farm implements I think this should be noted and drawn to the attention of the government.
May I also observe that these immense profits were made during a period when farm

Farm Implements Committee Report
implements were selling at comparatively low prices. In 1912, for instance, a six-foot mower, Eastern, was selling at S43.50; a six-foot binder, Eastern, S102; a six-foot hay loader, Eastern, S60; fifteen-disc seed drill, Eastern, $69. In 1937 the same machines had increased in price as follows:	Six-foot
mower, Eastern, S96.50; six-foot binder, Eastern, $225; six-foot hay loader, Eastern, $122; fifteen-disc seed drill, Eastern, $166. It will be noted that these priecs indicate an increase in the selling price running from 100 to 125 per cent over prices in 1912. In spite of that the farm implement companies again increased their prices on some lines of implements on November 1, 1937, the increase to take effect in 1938. Let us see how these increases compare with the prices of the commodities produced by the farmers. The index price, based on 100 in 1926, of all farm products in 1913 was 64. In 1930 it had risen to 86, and in 1937 the figure was 85. So 1937 shows a reduction of one point as compared with 1930, and an increase of thirty-three per cent over the index figure of 1913. How can the farmer stand an increase of 100 to 125 per cent in the price of farm machinery if he receives an increase of only thirty-three per cent in the price of his own products in the same given period.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) said this afternoon that one of the problems facing the government was not so much to reduce the tariff on farm implements or to take other steps to reduce the price of farm implements, but rather to increase the purchasing power of the farmer. May I say at this juncture that the hon. member for Greenwood is simply suggesting that the increased buying power of the farmer should be used to enable him to buy machinery produced on a protected basis. But how can that be done? The farmer in this country has a surplus of products which has to be sold on the markets of the world and in competition with the products of other countries. Consequently, on the one hand he is compelled to sell on a world-wide competition, while on the other those on the opposite side of the house would require him to buy on a protected market the implements necessary to his production.
Let me point out that from 1930 to 1936 many farmers had to write down their invested capital, and the amount of money which was borrowed by them had also to be reduced in many instances in order to enable them to stay on their farms. Might not the manufacturer of agricultural implements be asked to write down his capital investment

correspondingly during a period of crisis, or be asked at least to arrange that profits should be paid only upon the real capital investment and not upon stock issued during periods of expansion? He might be enabled thereby to reduce the price of machinery.
The hon. member for Greenwood also said that the farmers of Canada have played a noble part in the development of our country and that they will gladly pay a few dollars more to help their fellow citizens who are working men. I do not doubt that they have done so in the past; indeed I am sure they have done it, and I am quite positive they are willing to play the game again in the future, but not to give larger profits to manufacturers of implements or any other products upon an unreasonable capital set-up. Consequently, I would ask the government to take means through the tariff structure not only to bring back these companies to reason but also by suitable measures to restore and secure to the farmer the ability to obtain his implements of production at the lowest possible prices. Canada will be prosperous if its farmers are prosperous.
In concluding these very brief remarks, I take pleasure as representative of an agricultural county, in supporting the report of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston), and in asking the government to take whatever steps are practicable to secure in future for the farmer his implements of production at the lowest prices possible.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
The debate on this subject is taking considerable time, but I feel that I should say a few words upon some of the questions which have been discussed.
As regards the remarks of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), some hon. members interjected that no one would sell cream at eighty cents a can. In many parts of western Canada cream has been sold at seventy-five cents a can, and eggs at five cents a dozen, so that it has been extremely difficult for the farmer to live, especially during the depression years. It is certainly true that the farmer is kept solvent not by -his gross but by his net income. If the prices of farm machinery must be just and equitable, so should the prices of the farmers' production.
The speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was excellent in spots, and delivered with his usual force and precision. But I should like to remind him that it takes time for any policy or the benefits of that

Farm Implements Committee Report
policy to develop, and the report shows that when benefits are being obtained from a policy it frequently happens that the policy is changed or at any rate the underlying conditions are changed. Three years have now elapsed since the commencement of the agricultural investigation by the original committee; practically two years have gone by since the special committee first began to investigate the price of farm implements, and conditions have certainly changed during that time. I should like to read a little piece from the Manchester Guardian with regard to conditions on the North American continent since September, 1937:
The severe slump in American business activity, which started in September of last year, wiped out the gains of a three-year industrial recovery within the brief period of four months Many vague reasons have been put forward to explain this unparalleled decline, but it has now become evident that it was primarily due to (a) sharply rising costs and price disparities.
These have been largely discussed in the reports given by various members of the committee.
(b)	Excessive inventories.
There is no doubt that inventories of farm implements have been increasing especially when the purchasing power of the farmers has been so low.
(c)	Labour troubles.
That applies especially to the United States.
And in both countries:
(d)	Ever-increasing taxes. . . .
The downward trend was temporarily checked in January, and many administration experts confidently predicted that the depression had run its course. But the lull proved short-lived, and by the beginning of February trade indices showed signs of renewed recession. Some industries, such as utilities, building, and retail trade, whose business had held up extremely well, fell back rather sharply. . . .
The most serious obstacle to any recovery is to be found in the inventory situation. There is no doubt that the over-rapid piling up of inventories at the beginning of last year, as a protection against inflationary price advances and labour troubles, created a most unhealthy industrial boom, which people mistook for real prosperity. Although good progress has been made in the reduction of these excessive stocks, they are still out of line with current consumption in many industries.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thor-son) spoke at length upon the cream separator industry. I should like to touch upon this subject, because it affects so many people in my constituency. One of the most important sources of revenue for the farmers
not only in Alberta but all over Canada is the cream cheque. While it may be true that large dairy farmers who are milking quite a number of cows with the intention of selling the cream after separation may not regard the price of a separator as high, many of our farmers are dependent upon a few cows, and the cost of a separator means much to them, especially when their cream cheques do not amount to more than $150 anually and, as I suggested at the beginning of my remarks, when the price of cream becomes at times so low. These farmers usually raise large families and depend upon them for assistance around their farms. The cream cheques of these farmers are too small to enable them to pay high prices for their cream separators.
There is no doubt that tariffs increase the prices of home manufactured articles, or why would the manufacturers fear the competition in>
the dairying industry of the Viking and other imported separators. In the investigation it was found1 that prices of implements frequently rise because of the increase in the cost of raw material, which may be brought about by rearmament or other factors. But it is equally evident to the committee that excessive inventories and excessive capitalization increase the prices of articles within the country. It seems to me that if the tariff were lower, Viking and other makes of separators could be delivered in this country at a reduced price. We in the west realize that the country must have revenue to carry on its development and at the same time assist in creating local markets for our products. Hon. members realize that the consumer eventually pays the duty, and that wherever the consumer lives, whether in the east or the west, he is indirectly contributing to the revenue of the government. No objection can be taken to a tariff that affords industries indigenous to Canada reasonable protection against competition from low wage countries. It is strange to hear some members of the Liberal party advocating a higher tariff and others a lower tariff. Certain provinces gain by the tariff; others lose by it. This inequality should be offset by some form of compensation for those which lose by the tariff. Canada's national tariff policy is costing the prairie provinces much more than it should, because the price increase occasioned by duties is a burden that western people find it hard to bear. It is both short-sighted and inaccurate to say that the prairie provinces have brought their present troubles on themselves by their own action, and that it is up to the west to work out its own solution. I
2596	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
should like to quote from an article which I wrote myself some time ago on the national policy of Canada:
Canada is admittedly a difficult country to govern, as its geographical configuration suggests. What pleases one part of Canada frequently displeases another part. Tariffs are difficult to adjust with any degree of satisfaction all around. When the national policy was brought down in the budget of 1879 it was made abundantly clear that it was designed, as its name implies, to confer benefits upon the varied interests of the entire dominion. The government of the day denied in the strongest terms that it was intended to confer special advantages upon any one section of the country. On the contrary it was calculated to strengthen, revive and create manufacturing industries in all the provinces of the dominion, thereby establishing, it was declared, a larger home market for agricultural products in each and all of the provinces. Such were the motives and purposes of the national policy. But what do we find? To-day western Canada is suffering for want of local markets.
In pre-depression days the purchasing power of the prairie provinces contributed substantially to t)he industrial employment and general prosperity of eastern Canada. In fact, it was only with the development of the west that eastern Canada began to prosper. In the west there has been overemphasis in the past on wheat production. Less work is expended for the amount of returns in large scale wheat production than in any other branch of farming. Consequently, when mixed farming became general, western people took a deeper interest in the price of farm implements, such as the cream separator, used in this work. It is all very well to talk about raising the prices of farm machinery because you have to increase the wages of the employees, but when these men enjoy life through higher wages the farmers should be able to enjoy life because of the better demand and better prices for their products. So, if it is necessary to raise the price of machinery, some measure of justice should be done the farmers by raising their prices. These prices must bear some relation to costs. So long as manufacturers' prices are falling they can regard prices for their products with equanimity. Naturally manufacturers' costs do fall with the introduction of more efficient labour-saving devices. This enables them to sell at a lower price with a sufficient margin of profit, thus benefiting the consumer. Our farmers are mostly small scale producers who cannot employ large labour-saving machinery in order to reduce their costs to a minimum. Their standard of living is lowered because of these things, and they cannot purchase the machinery which the manufacturers produce.

It was stated by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) that all groups in the house had sufficient representation on the committee, especially the special committee. But I am very sorry to say that the members of the committee were not selected for their representation of agricultural areas. I should like to commend all the members of the committee for their long-suffering patience in hearing the tremendous amount of evidence submitted. But, on looking over the names of those forming the special committee, I find an unusual situation in regard to representation by provinces. We find one member from Nova Scotia, two from New Brunswick, three from Manitoba, three from Quebec, six from Ontario, seven from Saskatchewan, three from British Columbia, and none from Alberta or Prince Edward Island. Looking at the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon), if the Liberals wanted to put on the committee a Liberal from Alberta they might have chosen him. This all seems strange when we consider that Alberta is one of the largest mixed farming areas in all Canada. It seems to me that that province should have received more recognition in regard to the committee personnel.
It is well known that many Liberals advocate the raising of prices by means of tariffs, and many propose to lower prices by lowering tariffs. The choice offered to the free and enlightened elector is twixt Tweedledum and [DOT] Tweedledee. In that regard I should like to read a short extract from a speech delivered in the session of 1937 by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in regard to this question as we have observed it this afternoon, when we saw certain members of the same party sniping at each other as to what is best in the interests of the farmers in regard to tariff policy on farm implements. It is strange that after we have an expert committee investigating, and experts giving their views to this committee, we are no further advanced, because evidently they have not persuaded any hon. member whether he should vote for high or low tariffs, or whether the agricultural implement companies are dealing justly with the farmer. Speaking towards the end of last session the right hon. leader of the opposition said, as reported at page 2924 of Hansard for 1937:
In the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, in taking my seat I can only congratulate the government upon this masterly demonstration of their ability to hold under their banners troops who are marching to different objectives; who in times past marched shoulder to shoulder in a battalion to accomplish the defeat of a common enemy; and who, that victory having been won,

Farm Implements Committee Report
find it no longer pleasant to reflect upon that past, and instead of fighting shoulder to shoulder, are now fighting back to back, not for the purpose of destroying protection but for the purpose of rendering some assistance to a downtrodden country. And in the meantime the consumer who is not a member of the league can but hope some day to join it.
Every effort is made to rivet the attention of the public on tariffs, while crisis succeeds crisis and the mortgagee grips the land with ever greater tenacity. Political democracy is beginning to perceive that its very life depends upon winning economic democracy. The equitable distribution of opportunities, income and property within our nation will not only ensure internal peace and progress but, by the diminished pressure of the need for external markets for our goods and capital by reason of the increased volume of home consumption, will abate the perils of international conflict. The productivity of brains in industry and agriculture has hitherto found lucrative vent in supplying the growing needs of a rapidly increasing population, but the disastrous collapse of industry and employment since 1929 has made it evident that full recovery demands higher wages and more leisure for labour together with an expansion of public expenditure on works and services calculated to reduce the profits of capital.
I trust that something good will come out of the discussion which has taken place in the house with regard to this investigation into the prices of farm machinery, and that these prices to the farmer will be reduced to conform to the prices of the products which the farmer has to sell. Because there is no just relationship between the prices at which the farmer has to sell and the prices he has to pay for manufactured articles, a great deal of unrest has developed in Canada. That is not good for the country. A better situation can be brought about only when the farmers, who are the back-bone of the country, live in a certain state of economic independence.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read and studied the report of the special committee appointed by the house to investigate the prices of farm implements, and I agree with the recommendations of that committee. It is quite true that the committee was composed of men inclined to be sympathetic to the best interests of farmers; but no fault should be found with that, because if the house would legislate and do more in the interests of the farmers there would not be very much wrong with the implement industry. That industry would be prosperous, because, as the farmers of this country become prosperous, there is 51952-165
no doubt that the number of men employed in the manufacture of implements will be very greatly increased.
Abuses creep into every business and industry as time goes by, and I am quite sure there are some in the farm implement business. For some thirty-five years I have been engaged in the retail end of that business. I do not pretend to know anything of what it costs to make an implement; but I do know something about the retail side of the business, which has to do with the cost of distribution, because in the price of all farm machinery a certain amount is allowed for agents' commission. Sometimes, when the companies find competition pretty keen, they perhaps employ too many salesmen, and in the set-up of the implement companies I think there is one weakness. They have two separate departments, a sales department and a collecting department, and the one has little or no sympathy with the other. The salesmen are instructed by the company to go out and sell as much as they can, which is a very natural thing to do. Then, in the fall of the year, if conditions happen to be bad, they put on more collectors, and those collectors are out to get every possible cent. Some of the makers of farm implements in this country are not running their own business at the present time; they find themselves in financial difficulties. To-day one of the biggest manufacturers of farm implements is in the hands of one of the great financial houses of Canada. These people know little or nothing about the troubles of the farmer, and they are going to collect every cent possible; that is their business.
I believe that in the early days of this business some of the companies did make money. I know the United States companies doing business in this country are pretty well financed; they are pretty strong and are able to stand a few years of depression. On the other hand, I believe some of the Canadian companies are not in a very good financial position. They may have made good profits in the past; there may be too much water in their set-up at present-I know nothing about that-but they are in difficulties to-day, and I am not sure that the removal of the 7| per cent protection which they now enjoy is going to improve the situation very much or reduce the price to the farmer. I am just a little afraid that it will not do all that the house is expecting it to do. However, since abuses have crept into the industry, and since this is about the only weapon the house has available, I shall have to support the recommendation of the committee if they advise the abolition of that protection.

2598	COMMONS
Farm Implements Committee Report
That is particularly true with regard to cream separators. My good friend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) was not in error when he said that five gallon cans of cream were sold for eighty cents. I saw them being sold for that amount, at a time when manufacturers of cream separators in this country were enjoying the very highest protection, though the farmers were getting the lowest revenue they had received in years. Such conditions cannot continue, and if this committee recommends something that appears a little drastic it is not to be wondered at.
The complaint has been made that the cost of repairs is too high. It is true that repair parts cost more than the parts which go to make the complete machine, but there is no doubt that repair parts should be somewhat higher. It takes an army of men to look after these repair parts. I think I am not exaggerating when I say that in the city of Winnipeg to-day there is between 8500,000 and SI ,000,000 worth of repair parts, and it costs a great deal of money to carry them. The best machine in the world is no good if it is standing broken down in a field of wheat, and there is no repair part within fifty or a hundred miles. These parts must be kept at the shops of the agents if they are to be of any service to the farmers. That costs money; it means express charges, and there must be a man on hand who knows his business. They change these machines so often that it almost requires an expert to get the right parts.
Someone has suggested that the machines should be standardized. Apply that to any other business in this country and see what you get. For example, try to apply it to ladies' wearing apparel and see how far you can go. If the machines were standardized and every company could make the same kind of wheel or boxing or gear, there would be no competition. What would be lost in quality might be saved in price, but that does not help you on a harvest day when a machine is broken down and you cannot get it to give service. It costs money to carry all the repair parts.
Someone has said that distribution charges are too high. They may be. But I wish to point out that no one knows to-day how many binders, how many threshing machines, how many tractors or how many machines of other kinds will be needed to harvest Canada's crops this year. If those crops are heavy a great deal of machinery will be required. That stuff cannot be made in July and August; if we wait until that time it will be too late. The warehouses must be filled

with goods ahead of time. The machinery must be placed at strategic points throughout the country if it is going to be of any use to save the crops which it is hoped we will harvest, in view of sufficient moisture in the western provinces.
In 1915 I was in the implement business, and as part of my business I supplied binder twine. I do not know where the crop of that year came from. I thought it was a short one, but I do know that we sold more twine in that	year than	we	had sold in any	yearbefore.	We could	not	get the twine in	Canada. I	was agent	for	the International	Harvester	Company.	I	would telephone	our
office at Brandon, and every second day the express car on the train of the Great Northern, which ran through Boissevain to Brandon, would bring us 10.000 pounds of twine. Had it not been for that supply we would not have harvested the crops. There was at the time no company in Canada which could supply the twine in sufficient quantities. We happened to be on a branch line where we had good service with St. Paul and Minneapolis, and we succeeded in getting our twine every second night.
As I have said before, no one knows what the crop in Canada this year will be. If we are to harvest it and save it, we must have machinery stored at certain points where the harvest is likely to be heavy. It costs money to do that. I have made these statements in favour of the implement companies. Possibly, if the committee had sat down with the different farm implement manufacturers and asked them about their problems, some better arrangement might have been reached.
In 1931, when I saw the price of farm produce going down to a point where I knew the farmer could not pay high prices for farm implements, I wrote the International Harvester Company and the John Deere Company, for which I acted as agent, and pointed out that if they wished to keep the good will of the farmer the best thing for them to do was to reduce their prices by at least 25 per cent. I gave as a reason that the farmer would not be able to buy unless a big cut was made in the price of implements. He was not receiving prices which would permit him to pay high prices. However, they both wrote the same kind of reply in which they stated that they were confronted with the high price of labour and materials in the implements they had1 to sell.
I know it would not be wise to accept and I know that no manufacturing company would accept, as a long term policy, one which stipulated that it should sell goods below

Farm Implements Committee Report
cost of production. But I must point out to the house that the crop harvested in 1930 cost just as much to grow as crops for which the farmers received $1.25, $1.50 or $1.75 a bushel. For the 1930 and later crop they had to take a dollar, seventy-five cents and sometimes as low as twenty-five cents a bushel at points where freight rates were high. As is pointed out in the report, in order to retain the good will of the farmer I believe the manufacturers of farm implements should1 not have advanced their prices.
May I point out, however, that manufacturers of farm implements are not the only big business men who have made mistakes. The pulp and paper industry of Canada is suffering to-day because it got into the hands of big financiers, with a resulting over-production. Our flour milling industry is able to produce three or four times as much flour as it can sell. If any Canadian industry becomes prosperous, the financial interests are only too quick to get hold of it. They buy at the most reasonable prices, turn around and sell to the country at twice the price, and then slip out of business. That has been done in many instances. It may have been done in the past with the farm implement business; I think it was, to some extent.
There are certain factors which enter into costs. The statement has been made that the implement manufacturers are not making better machines to-day than they did some years ago. I say that is not so. The farm implement people to-day have made just as much progress in the perfection of their products as have the automobile manufacturers. We know the advances which have been made in the automotive industry, and I know we have better implements to-day than we ever had. The people who make farm implements are really the farmers' best friends, except that, like everybody else, they may be selfish in that they would like to see the farmer prosperous because they know, when he is prosperous, they will prosper with him.
I believe the committee is within its rights in recommending that the makers of farm implements should take into consideration the fact that the farmer is their only customer, and a time when he is not making money is not the proper time for them to advance prices. They should be willing to take their losses along with the farmers; no doubt some of them have done so.
If I understood the hon. member for Greenwood correctly, I understood him to say that in the new finance plan the makers of farm implements were charging only two per cent per annum.

Mr. MASSEY; I said six per cent, and then one-quarter of one per cent for three months, which is two per cent per annum, making a total of eight per cent.

speechtext:
In the west it is seven per cent. In addition to that, on an eight-foot binder there is a penalty charge of $11. If a farmer buys a binder on the 1st of August he has to pay for it on October 1. In the meantime he has to pay forty per cent for it when he gets it; there is a penalty charge of $11, plus a seven per cent per annum charge. I can see quite plainly where the makers of farm implements have overcome the hardships of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. When a man buys a machine to-day, a price, which is not the cash price, is set. There is a penalty included in it. If he desires credit for one month, three months, twelve months or two years, he must pay the interest for that period as computed, and add it in the note. It becomes part of the principal of the note, and in that way when these companies appear before a board of review, or when a farmer seeks to take protection under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, they are not going to have their interest cut off, as it has been in the past.
No matter what we do in this house, these men will try to protect themselves. That is only human nature; we would all do it if we had the chance. I am not speaking for the makers of farm implements, because I know nothing about their business. I do know, however, that they perform a good service for the farmers, and I should like to see the farmers and the manufacturers of implements working in harmony. I will support any measure the house may see fit to suggest to protect the interests of the farmers, because in Canada I believe their interests must come first.

speechtext:
The farmers have also had other privileges with respect to their products extended to them by empire and foreign countries under the trade treaties. That is as far as this country can go in that regard. It is not the fault of the industrial workers if the world price of certain farm products is too low. Some other method of assistance is necessary with respect to this problem. The dog in the manger attitude of suggesting taking away the livelihood of industrial workers because the farming community is in difficulties does not make for national unity, and it is a pity that such sentiments should be expressed. The prosperity of this country depends to an equal, if not greater, degree upon the prosperity of the secondary producer, the worker in the secondary industry, and upon team work between the primary and the secondary producer. We cannot have unity by attacking one section of the community, and in this case the attack is on the industrial worker.
In a spirit of all fairness I urge that this parliament recommend that this report be referred, lock, stock and barrel, to the tariff board in an effort to free industry and the workers in industry once and for all from political persecution.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT PRESENTED APRIL 8, 1937
speechtext:
I
should like to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to advance as fairly as possible the attitude of the farmers of my constituency with respect to this question, but before discussing that point I should like to answer one or two arguments which have been advanced by those opposed to the report.
A determined effort has been made to minimize the importance of this problem. I realize perfectly well that no farmer would be misled by any of the fallacious arguments that have been advanced in the house, but in order that hon. members who are not farmers might have a true picture of the

Farm Implements Committee Report
problem I should like to place on record some of the figures and evidence given before the committee. In advancing the argument that " Oh, well, the problem does not amount to anything anyway; it is a trivial matter," one hon. member went so far as to quote from an article which appeared three years ago in the Nor'West Farmer, stating that less than three per cent of the money spent by the farmer is spent on agricultural implements. If that hon. member had taken the trouble to read the evidence given before the committee, he would have found that the article in question was absolutely in error. In connection with one item the article was just over $200,000,000 in error. Anyone who has followed the proceedings of that committee could1 not be misled by such a quotation. It seems to me, however, a matter of great regret that an unreliable article, containing an unreliable conclusion such as this, should find its way into Hansard.
What are the actual figures? By referring to page 1215 of the proceedings of the special committee it will be found that according to the last census the farmers of this country had something over $650,000,000 of their hard earned money invested in farm machinery. Since there are just over 700,000 farmers in Canada, this means that the average investment in farm machinery per farmer across the dominion is between $800 and $900. It is a well known fact that farm machinery requires replacement much oftener than anything else in which the farmer invests his money. His house, his barn, his fences are much more lasting than his farm machinery. I think it is quite fair and within reason to suggest that farm machinery must be replaced at least twice as often as any other permanent equipment in which the farmer invests his money. If that conclusion is correct, it means that the actual investment of the farmer in machinery is closer to 24 per cent, or, in other words, nearly one-quarter of his total capital investment. That being so, this is no small problem to our farmers.
I must apologize for bringing this matter up again, but I think it is important. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) to some extent discounted its importance, but I do not agree with that. During the years of the depression, from 1930 onward, the farmers of this country were unable to buy the implements they required, or even pay for the repairs which were necessary. As a result, a deficiency or a backlog, as it has been termed, which is conservatively estimated at $200,000,000, has been built up during the years. If one considers also the fact that the normal purchases of farm machinery
by Canadian farmers amount to $50,000,000 annually, one will see that during the next five years, if the condition of the farmers continues to improve, they will be buying close to $500,000,000 worth of farm machinery. Is it not an important problem to them in connection with what they must pay for that machinery?
The next argument advanced was that we are persecuting the manufacturers of. farm machinery by holding an inquiry such as the one recently concluded. Personally I do not understand such an attitude. Here we have an industry subsidized by parliament to the extent of more than the total wage content of the goods they are producing; yet it is suggested that we are persecuting these companies if we ask for an accounting, if we ask what they are doing with the subsidy, the protection or the benefit we are giving to them. I submit that an inquiry such as this is not persecution, but that it should take place periodically in regard to all subsidized industries in Canada.

speechtext:
I have a great personal regard for the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), and I am quite prepared to debate with him any other problem which may come before the house. But I have a message which I wish to deliver on behalf of my constituents in regard to the question now before the house, and I must say that I decline to be side-tracked.
The farmers in my constituency have often reminded me, and if I read my history aright I believe it to be true, that the whole theory of protecting and subsidizing industries in this country was introduced and given to the Canadian people on the theory that infant industries required subsidies in order to become established in their early days. A great many of the farmers in my county are commencing to wonder when this lusty child is really going to grow up.
By referring to the report one finds that with respect to the industry in Canada 75 per cent of the business in connection with selling farm machinery is done by four large companies. The International Harvester Company do 33 per cent of the business; the Massey-Harris Company, 19-2 per cent; Deere and Company, 12-2 per cent, and the Cock-shutt Plow Company Limited and Frost and Wood, 11-6 per cent. In other words, these four large companies are doing 75 per cent of the total business.

I should like to place on record as fairly as possible some figures showing the profits of these companies through the years. Time would not permit me to show the financial statements of profits of all of them, so for the purpose I have chosen the largest company, namely the International Harvester Company. Referring to the proceedings of the committee one finds that the International Harvester Company of Canada was incorporated in 1903, with an authorized paid up capital of $1,000,000, which was held by the United States parent company. What profits did that company make during the first ten years of its operations? On a capitalization of $1,000,000 the company made profits totalling $3,500,000, or an average annual profit during the whole of the ten years of 35 per cent. I do not need to make any comment as to whether or not that profit is a fair and reasonable one. The facts speak for themselves.
Then, during the next seven year period, from 1913 to 1919 inclusive, the company earned profits of 7-2 millions of dollars, or an average annual profit over the whole period of 18 per cent. Hon. members wishing to have those figures before them will find them at page 1224 of the report of the committee. It is obvious that a state, of affairs whereby there was an average profit of 35 per cent in the first ten years and an average of 18 per cent in the next seven years could not be permitted to continue. The companies would either have to reduce the selling price of their goods or increase their capitalization, in order to conceal the profits. What did this company do?
We find that in 1917 the practice of the company of making temporary borrowings during its heavy financing season was discontinued, and instead the capitalization of the company was increased not once or twice, but ten times. The following year, in 1918, the capitalization was again increased from $10,000,000 to $15,000,000. Notwithstanding these heavy increases in capitalization, the average yearly net profits over the whole period from 1913 to 1919 again held at 18 per cent. Once again no comment from me is necessary as to the fairness or adequacy of those profits.
For the period between 1920 and 1925 the company ran into rather serious times, and profits were materially reduced. The auditor for the committee stated that during this period a dividend of $3,000,000 was paid in 1921, and that in addition to this there was a definite retention of profits in the United States of America by the parent company estimated at over $4,000,000. There is some
[Mr. Cleaver.J
difference of opinion as to the actual profits earned for this period, but it would appear to be in the neighbourhood of five per cent.
Coming to the last period taken up by the committee, namely, that between 1926 and 1935, admitted profits were earned of $24,500,000 by the one company, operating in Canada. In addition to this the auditors for the committee stated there was a retention of profits by the parent company amounting to approximately $17,000,000, making a total profit, for the period 1926 to 1935, of $41,-
500,000.	I omitted to state that during the latter years the capitalization of the company was again increased, and in 1935 it stood at approximately $27,000,000. Imagine the capitalization of one company at $27,000,000, and it still being an infant company asking for protection! The company claimed that added to this capitalization there should be about $12,000,000 for machines produced in the United States plant and simply distributed by the Canadian company. To me it would make very little difference as to whether we considered the increased capitalization, plus the retained profits, or whether we disregarded both. But in order to be fair to the company I have added both of these to my computation.
If I read the statement correctly, the result is that the total profit earned in Canada by this one company, over the ten year period above referred to, from 1926 to 1935, would be $41,500,000. If we compute this on a capitalization claimed by the company, it shows a net profit over the period of just over ten per cent. On the other hand, if you wish to disregard entirely the profits retained by the parent company-and I urge that these should not be disregarded-the profits of the International Harvester Company in Canada over the last ten year period, ending in 1935, was 7-7 per cent. Did any farmer make any such profit during that period?
There is another matter I should like to discuss which I suggest shows conclusively the truth of the contention of the auditors to the effect that millions of dollars were retained by the parent company, and were not shown in the statement of the Canadian company, although actually earned by that company. In this regard it is only fair to say that the companies were not to blame, and certainly the farmers were not to blame. But some overzealous officials of the Department of National Revenue followed the dumping clause, or the value for duty clause, in the customs regulations somewhat too religiously. As a result we find a very startling state of affairs, one which is almost unbelievable. On account of our own tariff regulations we were

Farm Implements Committee Report
compelling the head office of the International Harvester Company to keep in the United States profits actually earned in Canada. How was that done? It was done in this way: The company found that they must bill machines built in the United States to the Canadian subsidiary at a price higher than they were billing the same machines to the United States plants. If they did not bill at that exorbitant price they were charged a dumping duty by our Department of National Revenue.
At this point I should like to read into the record a few of the questions put to and the answers made by the manager of the International Harvester Company. I read the following from page 417 of the proceedings of the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for the year 1936. Mr. Morrison was being examined in the following manner:
Q. Take a. $300 machine, a machine that you would invoice to the American selling company at $300, at what amount would you invoice that same machine to the Canadian company? Have you the answer?
.A. Yes. The price to the United States distributing company would be $300.
Q. Yes?
A. The price to the Canadian company would be $346.
Q. Yes. Well then, I suggest to you that the question I put to you a few minutes ago is correct; that on account of our tariff regulations you found it more profitable to make your profits in the parent company than to make them over here; you charged the Canadian company $46 more for that one machine than you charged the American selling company for the same machine?
A. You realize, Mr. Cleaver, that the price that we charged the Canadian company was one that we were compelled to price at.
Q. I realize that. I am not saying that you were wrong in doing it. I am saying that our silly tariff regulations encouraged you to do it?
A. The profits of the Canadian company, of course, are affected by the higher price that they had to pay for these implements than if they had been purchased at the same price as the United States distributor paid.
Q. Now, we have the figure on this one type of implement, let us have the figure on another type-a tractor. Take a tractor that would sell to your American company for $1,000; what would you charge the Canadian company for that same tractor during the period when there was the full twenty-five per cent spread. Just recall your evidence of yesterday.
A. Yes. I want to give you the figures. I will give you an illustration, Mr. Cleaver, based on a tractor that would be priced to a dealer in the United States at $1,000.
Q. Yes.
A. The American distributing company would pay $750 for that tractor, the Canadian company would pay $950.
Q. So that the Canadian company was charged $200 more money for exactly the same tractor than you charged the American selling company ?
A. That is correct.
Q. And once again I suggest to you you found it profitable to keep your profits in the United States and never to let the Canadian company make them?
A. I don't like the inference that might be taken from that statement that we found it profitable. It sounds like we had elected to do that.
Q. I am not suggesting that.
A. The way it turns out.
Q. Then shall we say necessary?
A. That is better, and that is the reason I have not subscribed to your statement.
That accounts for the fact that the auditor of the committee said that millions of dollars of profits were retained with the parent company of the International Harvester Company and did not show in the operating statement of the Hamilton company. I contend that we should keep this in mind when dealing with the set-up of this company and considering the profits which they have made.
The question then arises as to whether a reduction in tariff will operate to reduce the price of implements to the Canadian farmer. I should like to read a letter written by the International Harvester Company, the same company with which I have been dealing, to all its agents with respect to prices after the tariff reduction had taken place. This letter is dated Hamilton, May 8, 1936, and reads:
Subject: Price reduction on account of changes in duty
Changes in the tariff which became effective May 2, 1936, reduced the duty from 12J per cent to 7i per cent on most of the items in our general line which we import into Canada. Goods which are manufactured in Canada are, of course, in no way affected by this change.
We have on hand in Canada a stock of imported goods which represents a considerable part of our 1936 requirements. This stock was brought in at the higher rates of duty previously in force. Regardless of this fact it gives us great pleasure to pass the saving made by the duty reduction along to our customers.
You will, therefore, effective immediately, reduce prices, both wholesale and suggested retail in accordance with the attached list.
We suggest that this information be given to your dealers at once, using the first three paragraphs of this letter as the letter to your dealers.
Then followed a list of something over 100 implements. The argument has been advanced that implements are selling in the United States at practically the same prices as in Canada. The further argument is advanced that the amount of tariff protection is not being taken advantage of by the Canadian companies. I should like to refer to a report to be found at page 1266 of the report of the committee, containing particulars of some ten implements which were considered by it. In this report will be found particulars with refer-

If he is interested in having it, I shall be glad to give it to him privately. The difference between the United States and Canadian selling prices is 10-5 per cent for ten implements, and our duty is per cent plus an excise tax of three per cent. I wonder if that is just a coincidence, or is it cause and effect?
The argument has also been advanced that the companies are not making money; that they are suffering losses. I think the financial statement of the International Harvester Company that I have attempted to give since its incorporation rather answers that argument. There is one further piece of evidence that I should like to read into the record. At page 1230 of the report will be found complete particulars of the break-down in the cost of an eight foot binder, retailing to a farmer in Regina at $281. If you reduce that figure by the cost of freight amounting to $26.08, you have a net laid-down price of $254.92. That machine costs the International Harvester Company $22.62 for labour, a total of $71.06 for material, and for all overhead, $36.48. These are the company's own figures; they are not mine. In other words, the total cost to the company of that eight foot binder is $130.16. This is the binder that is sold to the farmer for $254.92. There is a mark-up of $124,86, or 95 per cent, on a machine costing the company $130.16. Are the companies making any money? Do they need the pro-
tection upon which they are insisting? I am not attempting to answer these questions; I simply give the house the figures and let the members judge for themselves.
There is one other matter to which I should like to call attention. On this particular machine the difference between the Canadian and United States selling prices is $31.40, whereas the total wage content is only $22.62. The tariff protection, even at the present low rate, is considerably higher than the total wage content of the machine. That makes me wonder whether all the speeches adverse to this report which have been given in the house have been made by hon. members who are really interested in labour. I wonder whether they have not been partly interested in capital?

Mr. Speaker, the report of the committee of inquiry on prices of farm implements shows that the average purchases of farm implements were largest in 1928 and 1929. The decline between 1930 and 1935 is chiefly due to the depression which hit this country. However, prices of farm implements were too high, even during the depression. On account of high protection, farm implement companies made unreasonable profits, at the expense of the farmer. Such a situation constituted, I dare say, real exploitation, and called for the utmost optimism, enterprise and industry.
It is a fact that the farmer, who could not sell his products, had to pay $263, $273 and $278 for a binder. Several companies were even asking as much as $281. No matter what the companies have to say about the cost of labour, of raw materials and of transportation, and about commissions to agents, they cannot justify themselves in the eyes of the people. They were responsible for the aggravation of the plight of agriculture.
What I said about binders also applies to cream separators. The farmer paid $107.58 for a certain type of cream separator made by the International Harvester Company and costing $41.72 at the factory. However, the trifling sum of $2.47 must be deducted for transportation.

The figures I have quoted are found in the tables published in No. 20 of the report of the special committee of inquiry. Therefore, I feel it my duty to draw the attention of the house upon part of the recommendations of the report which seem particularly appropriate to me:
It is the opinion of the committee that the cost of cream separators to the consumers should be reduced and with that end in view recommends that this item be placed on the free list.
Reduction in the tariff should, and does, in the long run, tend to lower the price level to the farmer, depending on the extent of free price competition in the industry. i The provisions of the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff Act affecting the importation of farm implements should be clarified and simplified.
The cost of credit to the farmer purchasing farm implements on time is excessive and the companies should take immediate steps to reduce these credit charges.
The profits to the farm implement companies on the sale of replacement parts is excessive and the price of these to the consumer should be materially reduced.
The increases announced by the companies in January, 1936, were not justified by an increase in manufacturing or distribution costs or by the financial results of the companies in so far as these were affected by the price level of farm implements.
Over the period 1891 to 1936 retail prices of farm implements have been maintained at too high a level as shown by the financial returns to the companies engaged in the industry, during that period.

I do not propose to add anything more to my remarks, Mr. Speaker. But whether one likes it or not, no practical solution to the important problem of farm implements can be found in theories and speech-making. Ideas remain fruitless if not followed by action. The excessive prices set by farm implement manufacturers are responsible for the long delayed economic recovery. In many instances during the last few years, the returns from a year's harvest proved insufficient to meet the cost of a binder, a mower, a cream separator, nay, even a plough. So what has taken place? Moral failure succeeded to economic misfortune. The discouraged farmer, who had found his greatest joy in hard work, left for the city to join the ranks of the unemployed on relief.
Let not the farm implement manufacturers ever forget that their duty in the first instance is to co-operate with the farmer. Are they not themselves dependent upon farming activities for their living? Do they realize that? If they do not, sufficient power rests with the Government of this country to bring them to reason. They will undoubtedly exercise it, in accordance with the evidence of Mr. J. K. MacKenzie, as reported on page 1288 of the minutes of proceedings and reports, No. 20, of the investigating committee.
The evidence of Mr. J. K. MacKenzie, representing the Caterpillar Tractor Company, shows that as a result of the removal of the duty on tractors valued at over $1,400 in January, 1936, the prices of its tractors to the Canadian purchasers were reduced by the amount thus saved to the company in duty. The reduction in price was $880 in the case of one particular tractor.
Mr. Speaker, should the manufacturers feel inclined to retaliate or to resort to combines, the Government would still be in a position to apply the law as contained in the Revised Statutes of Canada and thereby overcome their obstinacy.
